prompt: What does it mean for a molecule to be chiral?

choices.text: It is not identical to its mirror image
It has a plane of symmetry
choices.why: A plane of symmetry makes a molecule achiral. Chiral molecules have no symmetry plane in any conformation.

choices.text: It rotates freely about its single bonds
choices.why: Rotation about single bonds changes conformation, not chirality. Chirality is about whether the molecule matches its mirror image.

choices.text: It can be superimposed on its mirror image
choices.why: That is the definition of achiral. A chiral molecule and its enantiomer can't be placed one on the other so that all atoms coincide.

explanation: A molecule that is not identical to its mirror image is said to be chiral (from the Greek cheir, meaning "hand"). You can't take a chiral molecule and its enantiomer and place one on the other so that all atoms coincide.

prompt: Which feature tells you that a molecule is achiral?

choices.text: It has a plane of symmetry in some conformation
It contains at least one −CH2− group
choices.why: A −CH2− carbon can't be a chirality center, but a molecule can contain −CH2− groups and still be chiral, as 5-bromodecane is.

choices.text: It contains a hydrogen atom on every carbon
choices.why: Lactic acid has a hydrogen on its central carbon and is chiral. Hydrogens don't decide chirality; symmetry does.

choices.text: It contains an oxygen atom
choices.why: Propanoic acid (achiral) and lactic acid (chiral) both contain oxygen. The test is a plane of symmetry.

explanation: A molecule is not chiral if it has a plane of symmetry. A molecule that has a plane of symmetry in any conformation must be identical to its mirror image and must be nonchiral, or achiral.

prompt: What is a plane of symmetry?

choices.text: A plane that cuts through the middle of an object so that one half is a mirror image of the other half
A plane that cuts an object into two halves of equal mass
choices.why: A hand can be cut into halves of equal mass, but the halves aren't mirror images, so it has no symmetry plane.

choices.text: The plane of the mirror used to compare a molecule with its enantiomer
choices.why: That mirror is outside the molecule. A symmetry plane cuts through the molecule itself, dividing it into mirror-image halves.

choices.text: A plane that contains every atom of the molecule
choices.why: Being flat isn't required. The plane only has to divide the molecule into two halves that are mirror images of each other.

explanation: A plane of symmetry is a plane that cuts through the middle of a molecule (or any object) in such a way that one half of the molecule or object is a mirror image of the other half (Figure 5.2.1).

prompt: Which of these everyday objects is chiral?

choices.text: A glove
A coffee mug
choices.why: Cut a mug in half from top to bottom through the handle and one half is a mirror image of the other; it has a symmetry plane.

choices.text: A plain drinking glass
choices.why: Any plane cut through the middle from top to bottom divides it into mirror-image halves, so it is achiral.

choices.text: A plain wooden spoon
choices.why: A spoon can be cut lengthwise into two mirror-image halves, so it has a symmetry plane and is achiral.

explanation: An object with a plane of symmetry is achiral. A coffee mug has one: cut in half from top to bottom, one half is a mirror image of the other. A hand has no plane of symmetry (Figure 5.2.1), and neither does a glove shaped to fit it, so a left glove can't be superimposed on a right glove.

prompt: Which of these is chiral: propanoic acid, CH3CH2CO2H, or lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)CO2H?

choices.text: Lactic acid only
Propanoic acid only
choices.why: Propanoic acid's middle carbon carries two hydrogens, and the molecule has a plane of symmetry when lined up properly, so it is achiral.

choices.text: Both, because each has a carboxylic acid group
choices.why: The −CO2H group doesn't cause chirality; propanoic acid has one and is achiral.

choices.text: Neither, because each molecule is small enough to rotate freely
choices.why: Free rotation doesn't remove chirality. Lactic acid has no plane of symmetry in any conformation.

explanation: Propanoic acid, CH3CH2CO2H, has a plane of symmetry when lined up as shown in Figure 5.2.2 and is achiral, while lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)CO2H, has no plane of symmetry in any conformation and is chiral. Lactic acid's central carbon is bonded to four different groups.

prompt: A molecule has a plane of symmetry in one of its conformations but not in others. Is it chiral?

choices.text: No; a plane of symmetry in any conformation means the molecule is identical to its mirror image
Yes; it is chiral in every conformation that lacks the symmetry plane
choices.why: Chirality is judged for the molecule, not each conformation. Propanoic acid has a symmetry plane only when lined up as in Figure 5.2.2, and it is achiral.

choices.text: It is chiral half the time, switching as the conformation changes
choices.why: A molecule that has a plane of symmetry in any conformation must be identical to its mirror image, so it is simply achiral.

choices.text: Yes; the molecule must have a symmetry plane in every conformation to be achiral
choices.why: One conformation is enough. Propanoic acid has its symmetry plane only when lined up a particular way.

explanation: A molecule that has a plane of symmetry in any conformation must be identical to its mirror image and must be achiral. Propanoic acid, for example, has a plane of symmetry when lined up as shown in Figure 5.2.2 and is achiral.

prompt: Which of these is another term that has been used for a chirality center?

choices.text: Stereogenic center
Symmetry plane
choices.why: A symmetry plane is what makes a molecule achiral; a chirality center is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.

choices.text: Enantiomer
choices.why: An enantiomer is a whole molecule; a chirality center is a single atom within a molecule.

choices.text: Achiral carbon
choices.why: A chirality center is the cause of chirality, the opposite of achiral.

explanation: A tetrahedral carbon atom bonded to four different groups is referred to as a chirality center, although other terms such as stereocenter, asymmetric center, and stereogenic center have also been used.

prompt: How is chirality related to a chirality center?

choices.text: Chirality is a property of the entire molecule; a chirality center is the cause of that chirality
Chirality is a property of a single carbon atom, the chirality center
choices.why: A carbon atom isn't chiral by itself; it is the whole molecule that is not identical to its mirror image.

choices.text: The two terms mean exactly the same thing
choices.why: One describes a molecule and the other an atom in it: the chirality center is why the molecule is chiral.

choices.text: A chirality center is the only possible cause of chirality
choices.why: A tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups is the most common cause of chirality in organic molecules, but not the only one.

explanation: The most common, although not the only, cause of chirality in organic molecules is a tetrahedral carbon atom bonded to four different groups, a chirality center. Note that chirality is a property of the entire molecule, whereas a chirality center is the cause of chirality.

choices.text: C5 is bonded to −H, −Br, a butyl group and a pentyl group, which are four different groups
It isn't chiral, because the two chains attached to C5 are both alkyl groups
choices.why: Two alkyl groups of different lengths are different groups. A butyl substituent is similar to a pentyl substituent, but not identical.

choices.text: Because bromine is a large atom
choices.why: The size of bromine doesn't matter; chirality comes from C5 having four different groups.

choices.text: Because the molecule has ten carbons, too many for a plane of symmetry
choices.why: Size alone doesn't decide symmetry. Decane itself has ten carbons and is achiral.

explanation: 5-Bromodecane is chiral because four different groups are bonded to C5, the chirality center: −H, −Br, butyl and pentyl. The difference between butyl and pentyl isn't apparent until looking four carbon atoms away from the chirality center, but there's still a difference.

prompt: Why is methylcyclohexane achiral, even though its C1 is bonded to −CH3, −H and two ring carbons?

choices.text: Ring carbons C2 and C6 are equivalent, as are C3 and C5, so the two ring "substituents" on C1 are the same
Ring carbons can never be chirality centers
choices.why: Ring carbons can be: C2 of 2-methylcyclohexanone is a chirality center.

choices.text: The methyl group rotates freely, which averages out its position
choices.why: Rotation of the methyl group doesn't matter. C1 lacks four different groups because the two ring paths, C2–C3–C4 and C6–C5–C4, are equivalent.

choices.text: C1 has only three groups attached to it
choices.why: C1 is tetrahedral with four bonds: to −CH3, −H, C2 and C6. The problem is that two of them are equivalent.

explanation: The C1 carbon atom of methylcyclohexane is bonded to a −CH3 group, an −H atom, and C2 and C6 of the ring. Carbons 2 and 6 are equivalent, as are carbons 3 and 5, so the C6–C5–C4 "substituent" is equivalent to the C2–C3–C4 substituent, and methylcyclohexane is achiral.

prompt: Where does the symmetry plane of methylcyclohexane lie?

choices.text: Through the methyl group and through C1 and C4 of the ring
Through C1 and C2 of the ring
choices.why: A plane through C1 and C2 would leave C6 on one side unmatched. The plane passes through C1 and C4, opposite each other, so C2 mirrors C6 and C3 mirrors C5.

choices.text: In the average plane of the ring, with the methyl group sticking out of it
choices.why: The methyl group lies on only one side of that plane, so the halves aren't mirror images.

choices.text: Methylcyclohexane has no symmetry plane
choices.why: It has one, which is another way of seeing that it is achiral.

explanation: Methylcyclohexane has a symmetry plane, which passes through the methyl group and through C1 and C4 of the ring. This plane makes C2 the mirror image of C6 and C3 the mirror image of C5, and shows the molecule is achiral.

prompt: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is chiral. Which carbon is its chirality center?

choices.text: C2, bonded to −CH3, −H, the ring carbonyl carbon C1 and the ring −CH2− at C3
C1, the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: A C=O carbon can't be a chirality center: it has a double bond and only three attached groups.

choices.text: C3, the ring carbon next to C2
choices.why: C3 is a −CH2− carbon, with two identical hydrogens, so it can't be a chirality center.

choices.text: The methyl carbon
choices.why: A −CH3 carbon carries three identical hydrogens and can't be a chirality center.

explanation: 2-Methylcyclohexanone has no symmetry plane and is chiral because its C2 is bonded to four different groups: a −CH3 group, an −H atom, a −COCH2− ring bond (C1), and a −CH2CH2− ring bond (C3).

prompt: Which kind of carbon could be a chirality center?

choices.text: A tetrahedral −CH− carbon whose three other groups are all different
A −CH2− carbon in a chain
choices.why: Its two hydrogens are identical, so it can't have four different groups.

choices.text: The carbon of a C=O group
choices.why: A carbonyl carbon is bonded to only three groups, one of them doubly, so it can't have four different substituents.

choices.text: A carbon in a C≡C triple bond
choices.why: A triple-bond carbon is bonded to only two groups, so it can't be a chirality center.

explanation: A chirality center is a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups. Carbons in −CH2−, −CH3, C═O, C=C and C≡C groups can't be chirality centers: they either carry two or three identical hydrogens or are bonded to fewer than four groups.

prompt: Which of these alcohols is chiral?

choices.text: CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3
CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3
choices.why: The carbon bearing the −OH is bonded to two identical ethyl groups, so it isn't a chirality center.

choices.text: (CH3)3COH
choices.why: The central carbon carries three identical methyl groups.

choices.text: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH
choices.why: Every carbon is −CH2− or −CH3, and none of them can be a chirality center.

explanation: In CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (2-butanol), C2 is bonded to four different groups: −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CH2CH3, so it is a chirality center and the molecule is chiral (Worked Example 5.2.1). The other alcohols have no carbon bonded to four different groups.

prompt: How many chirality centers are in 3-methylhexane, CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH3?
explanation: C3 is bonded to −H, −CH3, an ethyl group (−CH2CH3) and a propyl group (−CH2CH2CH3): four different groups, so it is a chirality center. Every other carbon is −CH2− or −CH3, and those can't be chirality centers.

prompt: How many chirality centers are in 3-methylpentane, CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3?
explanation: C3 is bonded to −H, −CH3 and two identical ethyl groups, so it doesn't have four different groups. Every other carbon is −CH2− or −CH3, so the molecule has no chirality centers and is achiral.

prompt: How many chirality centers are in CH3CH(OH)CH(Cl)CH3?
explanation: C2 is bonded to −H, −OH, −CH3 and −CH(Cl)CH3, and C3 is bonded to −H, −Cl, −CH3 and −CH(OH)CH3. Each has four different groups, so both are chirality centers. The two −CH3 carbons can't be.
